summary: Lit in 1866 on a small island at Coos Bay's entrance; the present 1934 concrete light was deactivated in 2006 and the tribes have owned the island since 2013.

lens.where: Coast Guard Air Station, North Bend (per Oregon Encyclopedia)

structures.note: About 25 feet (7.6 m) high; blown up about 1936. The record's 13 m conical brick tower is not supported.
The nomination dates it to 1908; the Oregon Encyclopedia says it began operating 1 July 1909.

structures.type: reinforced-concrete octagonal tower attached to a one-story workroom
structures.note: The 1992 nomination places the fourth-order lens in the lantern room; the Oregon Encyclopedia says it was displayed at North Bend in 1993.
A high bridge was first built in 1898; the 1938 bridge replaced it.

staffing.note: The nomination says the station went to automatic beacon in the early 1960s.

access.note: Tribal land, not open to the public. The high bridge to the island was removed in 2013 to prevent unauthorized access.

facts.agency: Confederated Tribes of the Coos, Lower Umpqua and Siuslaw Indians (owner since 2013)

corrections.why: The nomination describes the 1866 tower as an octagonal iron tower about 25 feet high; brick enclosure came in 1896. No source checked supports 13 m.
The 1938 structure is the wooden high bridge to the island (nomination), not a lighthouse tower.
The archive gives 84 ft (25.6 m) above mean high water for the present light. The 1866 focal plane was about 75 ft above the sea (nomination). Neither matches 13 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The nomination gives 1908 for the wood-frame lighthouse; the Oregon Encyclopedia says it began operating on 1 July 1909 after an appropriation in March 1907. Both are kept: built 1908, first operation 1909.

notes_for_editor: Keeper dates disagree across sources and the story says so: Denning (nomination 1910s to early 1920s; archive 1909-1912), Barker (nomination keeper 1923-1939; archive first assistant 1925-1939; LighthouseFriends assistant in 1938), Harris (nomination keeper 1939 to about 1953; archive keeper 1935-1957; LighthouseFriends keeper in 1938), Shaeffer (nomination mid-1950s to early 1960s; archive 'Arthur C. Shaffer' 1957-1964). Thomas Wyman: nomination says first assistant for more than fifteen years in the 1880s and 1890s; archive gives 1891-1906. LighthouseFriends says Thomas Wyman Albee (archive head keeper 1925-1935) was Wyman's grandson; the family link is not used in the story. Automation: 1966 (Oregon Encyclopedia) vs early 1960s (nomination). Lighthouse dates: first lit 1866 (both agree); wooden lighthouse 1908 vs operating 1909. 1898 accident date: 4 June (nomination), July (Oregon Encyclopedia), just over a month before the bridge in July (LighthouseFriends); names differ (Joseph Younkers, Joseph Yonker; Mr. Caldwell, John Caldwell). The 1866 tower's construction: wrought iron (Davidson, quoted in nomination) or sheet-iron enclosed (Oregon Encyclopedia); record's brick conical 13 m is not supported. Lens location: the Oregon Encyclopedia says North Bend in 1993; a travel site (not read) says the Coos History Museum; the story uses the Oregon Encyclopedia only. The 1866 light's fog signal and the Daboll trumpet's years are from the 1900 report only (scan p. 226; printed page not read). Newspapers: the Salem Evening Capital Journal OCR garbles the captain's name, so only 'remained with the Arago' is quoted. No Coos County paper was found in Chronicling America; the 1881 and 1886 Coos Bay News items are used only as quoted in the nomination. The North Star loss (January 1912) in which a keeper's relative drowned is in LighthouseFriends alone and is omitted. The record's characteristic (Fl(3) W 20s) and passport-stamp flag are not checked and are left out of the JSON. Revised 2026-10-22 (resume): the 1898 accident names and date come from the nomination (4 June 1898), not from LighthouseFriends; LighthouseFriends names Joseph Yonker and John Caldwell, the nomination Joseph Younkers and Mr. Caldwell. The Oregon Encyclopedia names the 1934 contractor as R.J. Hillstrom, the nomination as Jake Hillstrom; the story gives both. The Coos Bay News item of 25 August 1886 is quoted by the nomination and is footnoted to the nomination, not to the newspaper. The 1891 captain's name is garbled in the OCR, so the story says only that he remained with the ship and that the paper credited his judgment and persistence with saving the vessel. The story no longer calls the 5 October report the first. The Oregon Encyclopedia gives the fourth-order Barbier lens to the 1909 wooden lighthouse; the story attributes it there.
